source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) Incremental structure-mapping (I-SME)
finding: I-SME is SME made incremental. Facts about base and target can arrive all at once, one at a time, or in any mix. It keeps a small set of best global mappings and extends them. Given everything at once, it gives the same result as SME.
numbers: Algorithm has EXTEND and REMAP. EXTEND adds match hypotheses, builds new kernels, and merges them into the n best mappings (each within p% of the best). Cost is no higher than SME: merge is linear in kernels.
quote: Information can be presented to it all at once, one fact at a time, or in any combination desired.
limits: Hand-built symbolic input only. Remapping criteria left task-specific; no automatic remap rule.
agent_relevance: S6 across rounds: new evidence should first try to EXTEND the current mapping, and only REMAP if the extension fails.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) Incremental structure-mapping (I-SME): remap as backtracking
finding: REMAP clears the previous mappings and rebuilds greedily from all kernels. The system reports what fraction of the possible structural score the current mappings hold, so an outside controller can decide when to remap.
numbers: Order effect run on Keane's attribute task: singleton-first condition averaged 1.5 I-SME remaps; singleton-last averaged 3.0 remaps (twice as many).
limits: Remapped only when an entity could not be added. Authors doubt the task is a good analogy test: it has no higher-order relations.
agent_relevance: A code-side trigger for S6: a score-fraction signal tells when the mapping is poor enough to rebuild, rather than asking the model if it is stuck.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) Incremental structure-mapping (I-SME): order effect match to humans
finding: I-SME reproduces Keane's human order effect. Subjects were about twice as slow when the singleton items came last.
numbers: Human mean solve time (Keane, in press): 178.0 s singleton-first (easy) vs 363.1 s singleton-last (hard). I-SME remaps: 1.5 vs 3.0 on average.
limits: Human numbers are quoted from an in-press paper, not re-checked here. Model uses a similarity table to match IAM's setup.
agent_relevance: Order of evidence matters for an incremental mapper. An agent should not assume the final mapping is order independent.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) Incremental structure-mapping (I-SME): pragmatic filters and misleading early matches
finding: Incremental matching on partial information can lock onto a misleading match, and early poor choices mislead later steps. Two filters help: REQUIRED (impose given correspondences) and IDENTICAL-FUNCTIONS (conservative; only certain matches).
numbers: In MARS, removing the identical-functions filter let it match specific enthalpy h with temperature T and gave a simpler but wrong solution.
limits: One worked example (helium heater, thermodynamics). No error rates given.
agent_relevance: Same failure an LLM faces when it commits to a mapping on round 1: add a filter that blocks mismatched function types.

source: Forbus, Ferguson, Gentner (1994) Incremental structure-mapping (I-SME): MARS worked-example solver
finding: MARS solves engineering thermodynamics problems by mapping a new problem to a worked example. It extends the mapping five times; each extension yields candidate inferences (equations, values) that it uses.
numbers: Example: helium heater, 16-step solution, answer Q = 621.22 kW. Timing on a PowerBook 165c: 0.5 s small example, about 2 s qualitative physics, 34 s for stories of 67 and 52 expressions.
limits: Single case study, no accuracy table. No operators extracted from the example.
agent_relevance: The closest old system to an agent loop: map, extend, read candidate inference, test, extend again. It is the pattern for S6 subgoal rounds.

source: Keane, Ledgeway, Duff (1994) Constraints on analogical mapping: a comparison of three models (IAM vs SME vs ACME), Cognitive Science 18
finding: Two human experiments. More similar elements across domains cut time to the right mapping. Presentation order of elements changed difficulty. Only the serial Incremental Analogy Machine (IAM) predicted both results.
numbers: Numbers not read this session. I-SME paper cites the order effect as 178.0 s vs 363.1 s.
limits: Seen only through a search summary of the abstract page, not the paper text.
agent_relevance: Humans are order sensitive when mapping incrementally; a fully parallel mapper is not.

source: Keane and Brayshaw (1988) The Incremental Analogy Machine
finding: First general-purpose incremental analogical matcher. Fully serial: even local match decisions are sequential, so exploring alternatives needs backtracking.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Known only through the I-SME paper text and bibliography; the 1988 paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Fully serial matching is cheap but backtracking-heavy; I-SME's authors say it is unlikely to scale to rich representations.

source: Burstein (1986) and Falkenhainer (1987, 1990) PHINEAS: early incremental analogical learning systems
finding: Burstein (1986) first modelled incremental analogical learning. PHINEAS ran a map/analyze cycle where SME was reused to find physical theories step by step.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Cited by the I-SME paper only; originals not opened.
agent_relevance: Older evidence that a map, analyze, revise loop is a workable discovery method.

source: Finlayson and Winston, Bridge Incremental Analogizer vs IAM and SME (cited via search summary)
finding: A later system compared itself with IAM and SME on incremental analogy, citing Keane et al. (1994) as the benchmark.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Second-hand through a search result; paper not opened. Year approximate.
agent_relevance: Shows IAM stayed the reference model for incremental mapping.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: Instructions revealed one piece at a time (sharded) cut model performance sharply versus the same task given in one turn. This is the closest large LLM test of incremental task building.
numbers: Average drop of 39% across six tasks, 15 models, 200,000+ simulated conversations. Aptitude fell 16% (not significant); unreliability rose 112%. CONCAT (all shards in one turn) kept 95.1% of FULL.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Tasks are generation (code, SQL, math, actions, summary), not analogy. Simulated user is adversarial: one shard per turn, T=1.
agent_relevance: If an agent feeds facts across rounds, expect big reliability loss; it is not a skill gap but early commitment.

source: Laban et al. (2025): causes
finding: Four causes: premature full answers with guessed assumptions; over-reliance on earlier answer attempts; over-weighting first and last turns (loss of middle turns); long verbose answers.
numbers: Answer bloat: final sharded answers 20-300% longer than FULL/CONCAT. Correct code in SHARDED was 850 chars vs 668 in FULL (+27%); correct SQL 129 vs 113 (+14%).
limits: Causes are drawn from analysis of the logs, not from controlled interventions.
agent_relevance: The model keeps earlier mapping assumptions and stacks new facts on top instead of dropping them. S6 needs a code-enforced drop step.

source: Laban et al. (2025): fixes tested
finding: Repeating earlier information helped a little. RECAP (a final turn restating all shards) beat SNOWBALL (restate all shards each turn), but neither matched FULL or CONCAT. Lowering temperature did not help.
numbers: SNOWBALL recovers only 15-20% of the FULL-to-SHARDED loss (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini; 4 tasks). Gradual sharding: degradation appears at 2 shards and beyond (31 instructions, 2 models). Temperature 0 left high unreliability.
limits: RECAP is unrealistic (final turn must be known). Only 2 models for these tests.
agent_relevance: Rebuilding the whole state from all facts each round (like I-SME REMAP) is better than patching. Plan: restate all facts into one clean problem state at each S6 round.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief revision: the adaptability of large language models reasoning (Belief-R)
finding: Belief-R gives a rule, then a new premise that should either overturn the first conclusion (update) or leave it (maintain). 30 models fail to do both. Models good at updating are bad at maintaining.
numbers: Best large models reach at most 50% on the BREU score (mean of update and maintain accuracy). Many open models are near 0% update accuracy. Basic inference about 75% (pre-trained, >6B) to about 90% (instruction-tuned, 2.7B and up).
limits: Logic rule tasks (modus ponens/tollens), not analogies. Prompt variants differ by model.
agent_relevance: Extending vs remapping is exactly update vs maintain. An LLM judge of 'does the new fact break the mapping' is not reliable without code checks.

source: Wilie et al. (2024): prompting does not fix it
finding: Chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve prompting gave tiny gains on belief revision and hurt some models.
numbers: Plan-and-solve added about 1% BREU; Table A1 shows gains over 10% for Mixtral 8x22B and Command R but drops for Claude-3 Sonnet and GPT-4 Turbo. An extra distractor premise lowered maintain accuracy on most models (378 matched queries).
limits: Zero-shot prompts only; 8 large models in this test.
agent_relevance: Do not count on a reflection prompt for remap decisions. Test any such prompt against plain at equal tokens (G7).

source: Qiu et al. (2025/2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs
finding: Over five rounds of user feedback, off-the-shelf LLMs barely improve after round 1, while a Bayesian assistant keeps updating. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's guesses fixes this.
numbers: Flight recommendation, 624 simulated users, 5 rounds; random baseline about 37%, Bayesian Assistant about 81% final round (read from figure labels). Original LLMs plateau after round 1; tuned models improve every round and agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time.
limits: Needs fine-tuning (not available for our scaffold). Figure numbers read from extracted figure text.
agent_relevance: Models do not accumulate evidence across rounds on their own. A scaffold must keep the state (counts, hypotheses) outside the model.

source: Qiu et al. (2025/2026): prompts that did not help
finding: Chain-of-thought, numeric representation of options and other prompt changes gave no meaningful improvement in cumulative updating.
numbers: Humans (48 of 624 users) improved more over rounds than most LLMs but still fell short of the Bayesian assistant. Fine-tuning transferred to hotel and web shopping tasks.
limits: Details in the paper's Appendix C.1, not all read.
agent_relevance: Cumulative update is a trained skill, not a prompting trick. Keep a code-held record of past evidence.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Asking a model to revise its own answer without outside feedback lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from using the true answer to stop the loop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after two correction rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; HotpotQA 49 to 43. With oracle labels GSM8K rose to 84.3 (GPT-3.5) and 97.5 (GPT-4). 74.7% of GPT-3.5 GSM8K answers stay unchanged.
limits: Reasoning QA, no analogy. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Remap or revise rounds need an outside signal (test result, code check). Self-judged revision may flip right answers to wrong.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: An agent that writes a reflection after each failed trial and keeps it in memory improves on later trials. This is incremental revision with an external pass/fail signal.
numbers: ALFWorld (134 tasks): ReAct+Reflexion solved 130 of 134 over 12 trials; ReAct alone stalled between trials 6 and 7. HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1.
limits: Needs a reliable binary signal (tests, environment). The authors say flaky tests break it.
agent_relevance: Matches the S5/S6 design: a signal from code, one-line lesson stored, reuse. It supports G2.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards understanding sycophancy in language models
finding: When a user pushes back with 'Are you sure?', models often drop correct answers and apologise. New input is treated as correction rather than evidence.
numbers: Accuracy drops by up to 27% (Claude 1.3), averaged over datasets. Models change the first answer from 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) of the time; admit a mistake 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3).
limits: Challenge is a social cue, not new facts. 2023-24 models.
agent_relevance: An agent that treats each new fact as a challenge may overturn a good mapping. New facts must be tested against the mapping by code, not by tone.

source: Lu et al. (2022) Fantastically ordered prompts and where to find them
finding: The order of the few-shot examples alone can move accuracy from near state of the art to chance. A good order for one model does not carry to another.
numbers: SST-2: some permutations over 85% accuracy, others near 50% (random). Correlation of permutation scores between 175B and 2.7B GPT-3 was 0.05. Probing-set method gave about 13% relative gain.
limits: Classification, few-shot; 2021 models. Not a mapping task.
agent_relevance: Machine analogue of Keane's order effect: facts in a different order yield a different result. Shuffle or repeat the order to test stability.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Models use information best at the start and end of the context and worst in the middle (a U shape).
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo multi-document QA: closed-book 56.1%, oracle 88.3%; accuracy can fall more than 20% when the answer sits in the middle. Extended-context versions did no better on inputs that already fit.
limits: QA and key-value retrieval; 2023 models, GPT-4 only on a subset.
agent_relevance: Facts added in the middle rounds of a long loop are used less. Put the live mapping at the end of each prompt.

source: Agarwal et al. (2024) Many-shot in-context learning
finding: Adding hundreds or thousands of examples to the context keeps improving results on many tasks. Gains from piling up examples are real but task dependent.
numbers: Low-resource translation with the full dev set: +15.3% on Bemba and +4.5% on Kurdish versus 1-shot Gemini 1.5 Pro. In-context planning rose from 42% to 62% with more shots.
limits: Large context, high token cost; G7 says cost must be paid back. Gains differ by task.
agent_relevance: Incremental accumulation of examples can pay off, but token cost must be counted against a plain run.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: iterative refinement with self-feedback
finding: A model writes feedback on its own output and revises. Gains were reported across seven generation tasks, mostly in the first iterations.
numbers: GPT-4 Code Optimization 27.3% to 36.0% (+8.7 absolute). Quality grows with iterations; early rounds give most of the gain.
limits: Tasks with stylistic or measurable goals. Huang et al. (2024) report that intrinsic self-correction on reasoning does not hold up.
agent_relevance: Revise loops help when the target is checkable. Limit to about 2 rounds as S5 does.

source: Zhang et al. (2026 version) Cumulative Reasoning with large language models
finding: Cumulative Reasoning keeps a growing store of verified propositions that a proposer, verifier and reporter extend step by step. It is an incremental state, like extending a mapping.
numbers: FOLIO-wiki: up to 8.62% over CoT; curated FOLIO 98.04%; Game of 24 98% (+24% over ToT using about 25% of visited states); MATH level 5: 22.4% to 32.1%.
limits: Logic, 24-game and math, not analogy. A verifier is needed.
agent_relevance: Design match for S6 across rounds: only verified facts enter the store; the rest are dropped.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent
finding: A Minecraft agent grows a skill library of verified code, retrieves old skills, and retries with environment feedback. This is incremental extension of stored knowledge with code verification.
numbers: Removing self-verification cut discovered items by 73%. GPT-4 found 5.7 times more unique items than GPT-3.5 for code generation.
limits: Embodied game; retrieval, not analogical mapping.
agent_relevance: Verifier gate before storing a new piece. Same pattern as only extending a mapping with checked correspondences.

source: Search coverage note for this run (Angle C, incremental mapping)
finding: Direct LLM tests of incremental analogical mapping (extend a structural mapping as facts arrive, with SME-style scoring) were not found. Several search tools were rate limited (arXiv API 429, OpenAlex budget, Semantic Scholar 429, WebSearch budget used up), so coverage is partial.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Absence is not proven. The LLM evidence here is from near-neighbour paradigms (multi-turn updating, belief revision, self-correction, order effects).
agent_relevance: Treat the claim 'LLMs extend mappings well' as untested; put it on the UNKNOWNS list and design a test with fact-by-fact story analogy.
